questions.prompt: The Euclidean projection of a point that already lies in a closed half-space is
questions.explanation: If the point satisfies the inequality, it is feasible for the projection problem and the objective \(\tfrac12\lVert x - z\rVert^2\) is already zero there. Nothing closer exists. Moving it to the boundary increases the distance. The origin is the projection only when the origin is the nearest feasible point. A negative multiplier is not dual feasible for the inequality, so the projection does not wait for one.

questions.prompt: Project \((5, 3)\) onto the half-space \(x \le 2\). The objective is \(\tfrac12\lVert x - z\rVert^2\). What is the squared Euclidean distance from the point to its projection?
questions.explanation: The point has first coordinate \(5 > 2\), so it is outside. Stationarity writes the projection as \((5, 3) - \nu(1, 0)\). The bound forces the first coordinate to \(2\), hence \(\nu = 3\) and the projection is \((2, 3)\). The squared distance is \(3^2 + 0^2 = 9\). Reporting \(3\) gives the multiplier. Reporting \(2\) gives the bound. Reporting \(5\) gives the original coordinate. The second coordinate is unchanged because the normal is \((1, 0)\).

questions.prompt: For the equality \(a^T x = \beta\) with \(a \ne 0\), stationarity of \(\tfrac12\lVert x - z\rVert^2\) says
questions.explanation: The gradient of the squared distance is \(x - z\), and the constraint gradient is \(a\). Stationarity puts their sum, with a free multiplier, at zero. The multiplier is free because the constraint is an equality. Nonnegativity would be the inequality case. Ignoring the constraint leaves \(x = z\), which meets the equality only when \(z\) is already on it. A zero \(a\) is the rank failure the formula excludes.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order that projects \(z\) onto the line \(a^T x = \beta\). Each step uses the previous result.
questions.explanation: The rank check is the license for a multiplier. Stationarity then expresses the unknown point through that multiplier. The equality determines the multiplier, because it is the only remaining scalar equation. Substituting back produces the point. Solving for \(\nu\) before stationarity has not yet related \(x\) to \(z\). Skipping the rank check leaves a zero denominator when \(a = 0\).

questions.prompt: Project \((5, 3)\) onto \(x \le 2\). The candidate is \((2, 3)\) with multiplier \(\nu = 3\) on \(x - 2 \le 0\). Which claims hold?
questions.explanation:
The residual \((2, 3) - (5, 3)\) equals \(-3(1, 0)\), which is stationarity with \(\nu = 3\).
• The first coordinate is the bound, and \(3 \ge 0\).
• The product of the multiplier with the slack is zero.
• The original point has first coordinate \(5\), so it is outside. That is why the multiplier is not zero.

questions.prompt: Project the point \((p, q)\) onto the line \(a x + b y = r\). In stationarity the projection is \((p, q) - \nu (a, b)\). The multiplier \(\nu\) equals
questions.explanation:
Stationarity is \((p, q) - 
u(a, b)\) on the line. Dot both sides with \((a, b)\): \(a p + b q - 
u(a^2 + b^2) = r\), so \(
u = (a p + b q - r)/(a^2 + b^2)\). Every name is used. On the declared ranges the denominator is positive and the multiplier is positive. The opposite sign projects to the other side of the line. Dropping the denominator leaves a quantity with the wrong dimension.

questions.prompt: A note projects \((5, 3)\) onto the half-space \(x \le 2\). Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The point is outside, so the inequality is active at the projection, and the projection onto the bounding line is \((2, 3)\). The multiplier in \(x = z - \nu a\) is \(+3\), not a negative number. Outside the half-space the inequality multiplier is nonnegative. A negative multiplier would step to the infeasible side of the line.

questions.prompt: Project \((1, 1)\) onto the line \(x + y = 6\). The objective is \(\tfrac12\lVert x - z\rVert^2\). What is the squared distance from \((1, 1)\) to the projection?
questions.explanation: The normal is \((1, 1)\), with squared length \(2\). The multiplier is \((1 + 1 - 6)/2 = -2\). The projection is \((1, 1) - (-2)(1, 1) = (3, 3)\). The squared distance is \(2^2 + 2^2 = 8\). Reporting \(-2\) gives the multiplier. Reporting \(3\) gives a coordinate of the projection. Reporting \(6\) gives the right-hand side. The negative multiplier is allowed because the constraint is an equality.

questions.prompt: The closed form that uses \((AA^T)^{-1}\) for projection onto \(\{x : Ax = b\}\) requires
questions.explanation: Full row rank makes \(AA^T\) invertible, which is the Gram matrix of the rows. The matrix \(A\) may be wide. Square is a special case, not the requirement. A zero row drops the rank and makes \(AA^T\) singular. The right-hand side \(b\) can be any compatible vector. It is not required to vanish.

questions.prompt: When \(z\) lies strictly outside the half-space \(a^T x \le \beta\), the vector \(z - x^\star\) is
questions.explanation: Stationarity reads \(z - x^\star = \nu a\) with \(\nu > 0\) when the point is strictly outside and the constraint is active. The residual points along the outward normal \(a\). It is not orthogonal to \(a\). That would be a tangent step. It is not zero, because \(z\) itself is infeasible. A negative multiple would step further outside.

questions.prompt: Project \((6, 2)\) onto the half-space \(x \le 1\). What is the squared distance from the point to its projection?
questions.explanation: The point is outside. The normal is \((1, 0)\), so the projection is \((1, 2)\) and the multiplier is \(5\). The squared distance is \(5^2 = 25\). Reporting \(5\) gives the multiplier. Reporting \(1\) or \(2\) gives a coordinate of the projection. Reporting \(6\) gives the original first coordinate. The second coordinate does not move.

questions.prompt: When \(a^T z > \beta\), the projection of \(z\) onto \(\{x : a^T x \le \beta\}\) equals
questions.explanation: Outside, the inequality is active and the multiplier \((a^T z - \beta)/(a^T a)\) is positive. Subtracting \(\nu a\) lands on the hyperplane. Adding \(\nu a\) steps the wrong way and stays outside. The origin is not the projection unless the formula says so. Returning \(z\) leaves an infeasible point, which cannot be the minimizer of the distance.
